notes.meaning: God gave this message in 520 BC through the prophet Haggai to Zerubbabel, the governor, and Joshua, the high priest. The Jewish people had returned from exile in Babylon, but they were still under Persian rule and had no king of their own. God spoke directly to their civic and spiritual leaders to guide the whole community back to what mattered most.

The Lord confronted the excuse made by the people that it was not yet the right time to rebuild His temple. They hid behind bad timing, perhaps waiting for easier days or misreading prophecy. God called them 'these people' instead of 'My people' to show His displeasure with their cold and selfish attitude.

God asked the people why they felt comfortable living in finely paneled homes while His temple lay in ruins. They managed to find the time and money to beautify their own houses, yet they neglected the house of God. Their actions revealed that personal luxury had pushed worship out of first place.

The Lord told the people to think deeply about their daily choices and what had come of them. The phrase literally means to set their heart upon their ways. God wanted them to connect their ongoing struggles with their failure to put Him first.

The people worked hard in their fields, but their harvests were tiny and left them hungry and thirsty. Their clothes did not keep them warm, and the wages they earned slipped away as if dropped into bags with holes. God showed them that withholding from Him brought emptiness and poverty rather than security.

God repeated His command for the people to examine their ways so they would not ignore His warning. Having seen the painful results of their neglect, they were called to change their direction. The Lord repeated this call to move them from guilt into practical action.

The Lord gave three clear instructions: go up to the hills, bring back timber, and build the temple. He promised that He would take pleasure in their work and be glorified by it. God delights when His people show their faith through practical obedience and heartfelt worship.

The people hoped for large harvests, but they gathered very little, and God blew away even the small portion brought home. He explained that this happened because His temple lay desolate while everyone busied themselves with their own homes. Self-centered living had cut them off from God's blessing.

God stopped the dew and rain, sending a harsh drought across the entire land. This dry weather withered their essential crops of grain, wine, and oil, bringing hardship to people, livestock, and all their labor. These struggles were not random accidents, but covenant warnings meant to awaken the nation.

Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the rest of the people listened to Haggai and received his words as the true voice of the Lord. They responded with reverence and holy fear before God. Because their leaders set the example, the entire community united in readiness to obey.

Haggai spoke with divine authority as the Lord's messenger and delivered God's gentle promise: 'I am with you.' As soon as the people showed a willing heart to obey, God met them with grace and encouragement. His promised presence gave them the assurance they needed to do the hard work ahead.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching notes that Haggai was a human prophet carrying a divine commission, rejecting the ancient idea that he was an angel appearing in human form.

notes.meaning: The Lord stirred the spirits of the leaders and the people, giving them the willingness and courage to act. With renewed hearts, they came together and began working on the house of the Lord Almighty. True spiritual revival starts when God moves the heart, leading His people to joyful, shared labor.

differ.view: Reformed teachers emphasize that people are unable to obey or turn to God until the Holy Spirit first renews their hearts and stirs their wills.

notes.meaning: The work began on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, just over three weeks after Haggai's first message. During that time, the people organized their workers and gathered the timber and stones needed for the task. Their fast response showed that their repentance was genuine.
